title: What happens after the angiogram?
narration: The angiogram is over. What happens before you go home? Recovery starts with checking the place where the catheter entered, then making sure you understand the result and your follow-up plan.
visual_direction: Open on motion in the first frame. Follow the catheter withdrawing inside the artery, then match-cut to a nurse’s gloved hand checking the covered access site. Reveal the title after the spoken question. Keep the camera close to covered tissue and equipment.

title: Closing the access site
narration: Once the equipment comes out, staff control bleeding where it entered. At the wrist, they often use a compression band and ease the pressure as they check the site. At the groin, the team may apply pressure or use a closure device. The way they close the site depends on the procedure and the patient.
visual_direction: Show two distinct route examples, never on one body at once. In the first, a band’s pad rests over the right thumb-side wrist entry. In the second, show only a small right groin window surrounded by a surgical drape, then a covered dressing. Keep the closure illustration conceptual and omit application steps.

title: What staff check
narration: In recovery, staff check your blood pressure and pulse, look for bleeding, and assess circulation in the hand or foot on the side used. Depending on the access site and how it was closed, you may be asked to stay lying down at first. Staff tell you when to sit up and walk.
visual_direction: Use a moving point-of-view track from a generic monitor to the access-site dressing, then to a clothed patient’s supported hand or socked foot. Use no recorded patient data or normal-value claims. Hold the bed in position until the nurse signals.

title: Understanding the result
narration: A clinician explains what the pictures showed and what that means for your care. They may discuss medicines and prevention, more tests, angioplasty, or a review for bypass surgery. Sometimes more assessment is needed because the pictures alone do not explain the symptoms. Ask when you will receive any results that are still pending.
visual_direction: Cut from a single illustrative angiogram to a fully clothed, modest clinician and patient or show only their hands and a result summary. Reveal the choices sequentially with equal visual weight. Use a separate second example for ongoing symptoms. No implication that all options are appropriate for every finding.

title: Before leaving the hospital
narration: Some people can leave after observation following a straightforward planned angiogram. Others need longer monitoring or a hospital stay, especially if they have been treated for a heart attack or had another procedure. Before you leave, ask for written instructions, who to contact, and whether someone should accompany you home.
visual_direction: Show two clearly labeled recovery paths using modest clothed figures or simple room cues. One moves toward discharge after observation, the other stays for monitoring. A generic discharge sheet enters frame. No transport rule or length of stay on screen.
on_screen_text: Written plan and a way home

title: The written recovery plan
narration: Your discharge plan should explain what to do about the dressing and activity, including lifting, driving and work. Ask which medicines to take and what has changed. A stent can change the medicine plan, so check with your care team before stopping or changing medicines prescribed after one.
visual_direction: Follow a paper or digital discharge summary as three large headings enter in sequence. Put an optional stent icon beside the medicines heading and keep it separate from the angiogram-only case. No drug names, doses or fixed time limits.

title: What to watch at the access site
narration: A small bruise or mild soreness can occur. Contact your care team promptly if pain or swelling increases, if the site becomes more red or starts draining, or if you develop a fever. The team can tell you how to get advice and what to do if the clinic is closed.
visual_direction: Start with a small stylized bruise in a minimal covered wrist inset. Transition to icons for increasing pain or swelling, drainage and fever. Use multiple skin tones or color-neutral symbols. Keep the contact wording clear and separate from the emergency card.
on_screen_text: Contact your care team about worsening symptoms

title: When to get emergency help
narration: Get emergency help for heavy bleeding, bleeding that will not stop, or a rapidly growing swelling at the access site. Sudden coldness, paleness or numbness in the hand or foot on that side also needs urgent attention. Severe chest pain or sudden trouble breathing are emergency symptoms too.
visual_direction: Use a high-contrast alert with large, readable symbols and text. Switch from bleeding or swelling at the covered access site to the affected hand or foot, then chest or breathing. Keep the emergency action visible across the scene. Show no blood spray or personalized first-aid steps.
on_screen_text: Get emergency help for serious symptoms

title: What follow-up is for
narration: Follow-up is where you can ask what the findings mean for your symptoms, how the medicines fit into your plan and whether another test or treatment is needed. If the team recommends cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack or angioplasty, the recovery plan can explain how to join.
visual_direction: Pull back from the discharge page to an appointment calendar without dates and a brief conceptual rehabilitation icon. Keep rehab tied to heart attack or angioplasty when advised. Avoid implying every diagnostic angiogram leads to rehab.

title: Before you go
narration: Three things are worth having in writing. What did the angiogram show? What is your plan for recovery and medicines? Who should you contact if you have a problem? The answers may be different for someone who had a test alone and someone who also had treatment.
visual_direction: Bring each question onto the screen as a separate moving beat. Finish with the two clearly labeled pathways. Keep the content free of patient data and use only the established Elysian mark and type.

title: Clinical sources
visual_direction: Hold the source and production card for eight seconds. Show the authentic logo, abbreviated AHA and NHS source names, the next episode title, and a short truthful disclosure of illustrative medical imagery and synthetic English narration.
